turn_text: Hey, thanks. It's good to be with you.
In taking this job, how do you relate to the boards and the members of these rural electric cooperatives?

Well, I feel pretty blessed because I represented Canada very rural district in Missouri and had nine co-ops representing most or all different pieces of that congressional district. So, you know, for the 17 plus years I spent in Congress, among my favorite people were always the boards of directors and members of co-ops who came to visit me and keeping in mind too that short of where I lived in a couple of municipal electricity systems, we had all co-ops. It's just like being in Congress but in Congress nationally if you know what I mean. I love these folks. I love them because not only do they care about their co-op, but they really do care about their communities. And they spend so much time involved in those communities, whether it's through the Rotary Club, Lions Club, local chambers, doing business incubators, finding other opportunities for job creation and economic development. And what's terrific about it is the way we used to do it in Missouri and the way we still do it in Missouri is somewhat similar to what you might see out in Oregon, for example, but because we have different regions that have different peculiarities, everything is a little different, but at the end of the day, people are very committed to the co-ops and to their members and really care about the lives and livelihoods of all of the folks they serve. And so that's throughout the entire system. and I feel pretty darn blessed to be able to work with people like that.

turn_text: Is there support in Congress to continue to assist real electric cooperatives to provide electricity and other services to those who live in the rural areas?

Oh, well, I absolutely, I absolutely think so. I certainly know that all of the former colleagues that I know who represent districts where there are co-ops are very involved with them and they spend a lot of time visiting their different co-op annual meetings and that sort of thing. And they feel very strongly that it's important to listen to their constituents. And certainly, you know, if you have a district full of co-op members, you're going to sure listen to them. And that's really good. And what I love is that We not only have our co-op members who come to Washington during our legislative fly, and some actually come three or four times a year, but they actually hold events and or invite members of Congress to visit the co-ops back home, which is where I think, which I think is so very important because then you get to meet all of the employees and really see how they run, which is You know, usually we don't have too many folks who have either worked in co-ops or been CEOs of them, been on the boards of directors, not too many who are in Congress today, but they listen to their co-op members at all times and that's really important for us at the national level because when you want to talk to a member about a specific issue, I always think it's best to have the folks from back home do the talking because they're the ones who are impacted by the policies that Congress is making.

turn_text: I'd like to finish up are the real electric cooperatives in conflict with the Obama administration on energy efficiency goals or any mandates coming out of Washington DC?

Well, I will say that with regard to energy efficiency in the Obama administration that quite frankly we are leading the industry on energy efficiency and have been doing and have been working on this for years. So we have There's no conflict with the Obama administration with regard to those issues. As a matter of fact, the Department of Energy has given us some grants to help some of the national labs and universities work on making even more efficient opportunities available in the near future. On mandates, well, you know, I think you can look at co-ops, you can look at IUs, you can look at small businesses, you can look at anybody, in the country, any kind of business. And when the government tries to impose a mandate, particularly when you're doing things voluntarily with regard to climate change specifically, with what we're doing with adding renewables and even more efficiency measures to each of our co-ops, if we're doing it voluntarily and we're leading the industry, it seems a little bit short-sighted, in my opinion, that you have an mandate slapped down and posed on you, particularly when the folks who are often doing these don't really understand the industry and or the ramifications. Because at the end of the day, we still represent, we represent people who are not necessarily capable of paying huge, expensive energy bills like Germany, for example. And so we're very cognizant and very concerned when some new rule comes down the road that would cause us to have to increase energy bills to the tune of, you know, double what somebody's paying now. When you're living on a fixed income, we have a lot of senior citizens who are retired in rural America, as I know you know. It's really hard to to have to pass along those costs. And we at the co-ops, we're all not for profit. And our members who are our customers actually own that co-op. And so you keep costs down. And it's pretty hard to ask somebody who's Social Security check might be going up about a third of a percent to pay an energy bill that to double what they would have paid last year. So mandates not a big fan of them, especially when we're doing things voluntarily and being way ahead of the industry on that front.
